lesson.title: Download and Disconnect: The One-Mailbox-One-Machine Model of POP3
lesson.summary: POP3 is an older mail retrieval protocol built around downloading messages to a single device, traditionally removing them from the server afterward, which stands in direct contrast to IMAP's server side syncing model.
lesson.body:
POP3, the Post Office Protocol version 3, solves the same basic problem as IMAP, getting a message out of a mailbox on the mail server and onto a device where a person can read it, but it takes a much simpler and older approach. Rather than treating the server mailbox as the ongoing source of truth that every device synchronizes with, POP3 is built around a download and disconnect model: the client connects, downloads whatever new messages are waiting, and traditionally deletes them from the server once the download succeeds, leaving the local device as the one and only place those messages now live.

A POP3 session is short and simple by design. After authenticating with a USER command giving the account name and a PASS command giving the password, the client can issue LIST to see what messages are waiting, RETR to download a specific message, DELE to mark a message for deletion, and QUIT to end the session, at which point any messages marked for deletion are actually removed from the server. There is no concept of folders on the server side, no flags synchronized back, and no shared view between multiple clients, because the protocol was never designed with multiple simultaneous devices in mind.

This is the direct contrast with IMAP from the previous chapter. IMAP keeps the mailbox on the server and lets many devices see a consistent, synchronized view of it. POP3 was built for a world where a person checked email from essentially one machine, historically often over a dial up connection, and once mail was downloaded to that machine, that copy was the only copy that mattered going forward. Check that same account from a second device after a POP3 client has already downloaded and removed messages from the server, and those messages simply are not there anymore, because the server was never meant to be the long term home for them. Many modern POP3 clients can be configured to leave a copy on the server for some period of time rather than deleting it immediately, but that is a configuration choice layered on top of a protocol whose traditional and defining behavior is to download and remove, which is exactly why IMAP, not POP3, has become the standard choice for anyone checking mail from more than one device.
